methodology: 1. ENERGY BALANCE FRAMEWORK: This programme operates on the principle of sustained negative energy balance. A deficit of 300–500 kcal/day below Total Daily Energy Expenditure (TDEE) produces a fat loss rate of 0.4–0.6 kg/week. This rate minimises adaptive thermogenesis, preserves lean body mass, and supports hormonal homeostasis. Faster rates (>1 kg/week) increase risk of gallstone formation, muscle catabolism, and menstrual disruption in females.

2. PROTEIN THRESHOLD: Protein intake is set at 1.4–1.6 g/kg target body weight (90g/day for 55kg goal). This exceeds the RDA (0.8 g/kg) and aligns with sports nutrition consensus for body recomposition during caloric restriction. Higher protein preserves muscle protein synthesis, increases diet-induced thermogenesis (DIT: 20–30% of protein kcal vs 5–10% for carbs/fats), and enhances satiety via GLP-1 and PYY secretion.

3. MACRONUTRIENT DISTRIBUTION: The 1500 kcal target is distributed as 24% protein (90g), 35% carbohydrate (130g), and 30% fat (50g), with 8% fibre (30g). This moderate-carbohydrate approach supports thyroid function, training performance, and cognitive clarity while maintaining sufficient fat for steroid hormone synthesis and fat-soluble vitamin absorption.

4. MEAL PATTERNING: Three main meals plus 1–2 snacks distributed across a 10–12 hour eating window (e.g., 08:00–20:00) supports circadian alignment. Front-loading calories (larger breakfast/lunch, moderate dinner) improves glucose tolerance and reduces evening hyperphagia.

5. FOOD QUALITY HIERARCHY: The programme prioritises whole, minimally processed foods. The NOVA classification system guides selections: Group 1 (unprocessed/minimally processed) forms 80–90% of intake; Group 2 (culinary ingredients) 5–10%; Group 3 (processed foods) ≤10%; Group 4 (ultra-processed) ≤5% (weekly treat meal).

6. BEHAVIOURAL ADHERENCE MECHANISMS: (a) Flexible eating: one weekly meal ≤800 kcal prevents psychological restriction and supports social participation. (b) Meal prep: batch cooking on Sundays reduces decision fatigue and improves adherence by 40–60%. (c) Self-monitoring: daily food logging increases weight loss success by 2–3x versus non-logging (Burke et al., 2011). (d) Progress photos: visual feedback maintains motivation when scale weight plateaus.

7. HYDRATION & MICRONUTRIENTS: Water intake of 2.5L/day supports cellular metabolism, thermoregulation, and appetite regulation. The programme emphasises food-first micronutrient acquisition through 5+ vegetable servings and 2+ fruit servings daily. Supplements address only documented gaps (Vitamin D in equatorial latitudes with high indoor exposure; Omega-3 if salmon intake <2x/week).

8. SLEEP & STRESS INTEGRATION: Sleep restriction to <7 hours increases ghrelin (+28%) and reduces leptin (-18%), amplifying hedonic food cravings (Spiegel et al., 2004). Chronic cortisol elevation promotes visceral adiposity. The programme recommends 7–9 hours sleep and stress-reduction practices (walking, journaling, prayer/meditation) as non-negotiable adjuncts to nutrition.

Before commencing this or any dietary programme, individuals should consult a registered medical practitioner or accredited dietitian, particularly if they:
• Have a diagnosed medical condition (diabetes, hypertension, kidney disease, thyroid disorder, eating disorder history)
• Are pregnant, breastfeeding, or planning pregnancy
• Are under 18 years of age or over 65 years of age
• Are taking prescription medication that may interact with dietary changes
• Have a history of disordered eating or body dysmorphia
